passage:
Sabina here. Raghav sits opposite me, and for months I noticed a small ritual: at half past five, before shutting down, he wrote three lines in a tiny blue notebook. I asked once. "Three good things from today," he said. "But specific. Not 'family' or 'health,' those bore me. Today: the cook put extra jaggery in my tea without asking, a client said 'that was clear,' and the pigeon on the sill finally left."
I laughed. But over the months he seemed to notice more and complain less at lunch. I can't say it's all the notebook. He also started pointing out good things to me, too. Yesterday it was "the printer worked first time." We celebrated with biscuits.

qa.q: What did Raghav write in the tiny blue notebook at half past five?
qa.a: Three good things from the day.

qa.q: What might Raghav be feeling at half past five when he writes his three lines?
qa.a: Content and attentive. Small, specific things like extra jaggery or a client's compliment seem to give him quiet pleasure.

qa.q: What makes Raghav's list work better than a general one?
qa.a: He writes specific, fresh items and avoids generic words like family or health, so he has to notice real moments.

qa.q: What does Sabina think the notebook has done for Raghav?
qa.a: Sabina thinks Raghav notices more and complains less, though Sabina cannot say it is all the notebook.

grounding: A young adult writes three specific good things at the end of the day and their attention shifts toward what works.

passage:
Day 1. Darshan wrote his first gratitude list: family, health, job. It felt like filling in a form, and he closed the notebook without feeling anything.
Day 6. His flatmate Manjula looked at the list. "Too generic," she said. "What made you smile today?" He thought. That evening he wrote: The fruit seller kept the ripe mango aside for me. My bus came just as I reached the stop. Manjula's terrible joke about the geyser.
Day 20. Walking to work, Darshan caught himself noticing the steam from the chai stall and a neighbour's rangoli, so he would have something to write. His shoulders had dropped without his noticing.

qa.q: What three generic things did Darshan write on Day 1?
qa.a: Family, health, job.

qa.q: What did Darshan feel about his first list?
qa.a: Flat and unmoved. It felt like filling in a form, and he closed the notebook without feeling anything.

qa.q: What turning point improved Darshan's list?
qa.a: Manjula said the list was too generic and asked what made him smile, so he wrote specific moments like the ripe mango.

qa.q: How might Manjula see Darshan's first list?
qa.a: As too generic to catch anything real, which is why she asks what made him smile today.

grounding: A young adult replaces a generic gratitude list with specific noticed moments, and attention shifts.

passage:
Maria, you asked how I stayed cheerful in that miserable first job in Bombay. At twenty-five I was a junior clerk in a shipping office, and every day felt grey. A senior, old Mr Pinto, saw me sulking and said, "Every night, write three good things. But they must be new and exact. Not 'family', not 'health'. Something from today."
So I did. "The canteen man gave me the cup with no chip." "A pigeon walked into the office and the manager laughed." "The rain stopped exactly when I left." By the second month I was noticing these things during the day, collecting them for my list.
The office didn't change. I did. Your Shankar Uncle still keeps that notebook.

qa.q: What was one of Shankar's three good things?
qa.a: The canteen man gave him the cup with no chip.

qa.q: How did Shankar feel at the start of that job?
qa.a: Shankar felt gloomy and sulky, with every day grey.

qa.q: Which of Mr Pinto's rules made the practice work?
qa.a: The good things had to be new and exact, from that day, not generic like "family" or "health".

qa.q: Why might Mr Pinto have given this advice?
qa.a: Mr Pinto noticed a sulking young clerk and wanted to help him shift his attention, perhaps from his own experience.

grounding: Shows a young adult writing three specific, fresh good things each night and finding attention shifting.

passage:
Maria's night shifts at the hospital left her too tired to think. Her counsellor had suggested writing three good things each day, so she did: "family, health, job". Every night, the same three words. After two weeks they felt like nothing.
Her brother Joseph, who shared the tiny flat, read the list and laughed. "That's a shopping list, not a day. What actually happened?"
So the next dawn, the bus rattling and her eyes stinging, she tried again. "The old man in bed six squeezed my hand and called me beta." "The chai stall had just boiled a fresh pot." "Joseph left the landing light on for me."
She noticed she had smiled writing the last one. The next evening, on the ward, she caught herself looking for things to write.

qa.q: What were the three words Maria wrote every night at first?
qa.a: Family, health, job.

qa.q: How did Maria feel about the repeated list after two weeks?
qa.a: The list felt empty and meaningless to Maria.

qa.q: What change made the practice work for Maria?
qa.a: Writing specific, fresh moments from the day, like the man in bed six and the landing light, instead of the same three words.

qa.q: Why might Joseph have left the landing light on?
qa.a: Joseph probably cared about Maria coming home tired at dawn and wanted to make it easier.

grounding: Shows a young adult finding that specific, freshly noticed good things work better than a repeated generic list.

passage:
Every night in their Bengaluru flat, before switching off the lamp, Ishita wrote three lines in a small green notebook. Her roommate Damini teased her about it. "Let me guess. Grateful for coffee, grateful for wi-fi."
Ishita handed her the notebook. Damini read: "Tuesday: the auto driver waited while I ran back for my ID. The code finally compiled at 4:12 pm. Amma sent a voice note singing off-key." "Wednesday: new bakery on 7th Cross, cardamom bun. My manager said good catch. The rain smelled like my school."
"They're all different," Damini said slowly.
"If I write the same things, I stop seeing anything," Ishita said. "This way I spend the day looking."
Damini went quiet. The next night, Ishita noticed a second notebook on Damini's pillow.

qa.q: What did Ishita write about the code?
qa.a: The code finally compiled at 4:12 pm.

qa.q: What was Damini feeling as she read the notebook?
qa.a: Damini went from teasing to surprised and quietly moved, noticing every entry was different.

qa.q: Why does Ishita avoid writing the same things?
qa.a: Repeated items make her stop seeing; fresh, specific ones make her spend the day looking for good things.

qa.q: What does the second notebook on Damini's pillow suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Damini was persuaded and decided to try the practice too.

grounding: Shows a young adult noting three specific good things each night and attention shifting toward what works.

passage:
"Lakshmi, what are you writing every night before bed?"
"Three good things from today. Specific ones."
"Like 'family, health, job'?"
"That's what I wrote the first week, Ujjwal. Same three every night. It did nothing. I got bored of my own list."
"So what now?"
"Now it has to be something from today that I actually noticed. Tonight: one, the autowala who waited while I ran back for my umbrella. Two, the new intern finally laughed at my joke. Three, the smell of rain on the terrace at six."
"That's oddly detailed."
"That's the point. I start looking for them during the day. At the bus stop I'm thinking, is this one of my three?"
"And?"
"And I'm less grumpy. I notice the auto waiting instead of only the traffic."
"Can I try?"
"Go. One from today. Specific."
"...You made chai without being asked."
"Good. That counts."

qa.q: What was Lakshmi's third good thing tonight?
qa.a: The smell of rain on the terrace at six.

qa.q: What was Lakshmi feeling in the first week of the practice?
qa.a: Lakshmi felt bored with the same generic list, which did nothing to change the day.

qa.q: What made Lakshmi's practice work?
qa.a: Choosing fresh, specific things from that day, which made Lakshmi look for good moments and shifted attention to what works.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal feel after naming the chai?
qa.a: Ujjwal might feel a little pleased and warm, noticing a small kindness and sharing it with Lakshmi.

grounding: A young adult writes three specific good things each night, finding that fresh, specific noticing shifts attention better than generic lists.
